knowledge_points.label: Post-training = imitation (SFT) then reinforcement (RLHF): collect the behaviours you want
knowledge_points.statement: Pretraining data scales but is not the behaviour we want from a model, so post-training collects data of the behaviours we do want and trains on it in two stages: supervised fine-tuning (imitation of demonstrations) followed by reinforcement from human feedback (optimizing a reward built from preferences); the lecture's three questions are what that data looks like, how to use it, and whether it needs scale.

anchors.quote: Pretraining data isn't quite what we want (but it scales).. ... Can we collect data of behaviors we do want and train the LM?
1. What does that data look like? 2. How do we best make use of that data? 3. Do we need scale for this?
Standard approach – imitation (SFT) followed by reinforcement ('RL' HF)
We've now covered pre-training, which gets you to GPT3.. But how do we get to instructGPT?

pre-training is always important. ... if we ignore pre-training and we just try to train our way to victory, we will get none of the things that we want. ... we have to then extract the kinds of behaviors that we want out of this kind of primordial soup that is pre-training.

algorithms are not really the secret sauce. ... It's going to be the data. ... The first part is you go and collect some demonstration data. ... Then after you have that, you're going to do some reinforcement learning of some kind
We all how to SFT a model. That's basically exactly the same as pre-training. So the only real difference with some minor variation is going to be the training data.

information about frontier post-training is honestly pretty sparse in many, many ways. ... the RLHF paper, learning to summarize from human feedback, that's actually incredibly detailed. ... The data is very much a trade secret.

provenance.filtering_note: The InstructGPT three-step figure on p6 and p31 is an image; only the caption '[Ouyang 2022]' survives, so the reward-model step between SFT and PPO is named here from the paper, not the text layer. p3 motivates the whole lecture with a Bubeck et al. 2023 instruction-following example (image). p5 is the professor's caveat that modern post-training information is sparse (open source: 'lots of distillation, not too public in open-source release notes'; closed source: 'secret sauce'), with Stiennon 2020 and Bai 2022 named as the rich pre-ChatGPT sources; the deck therefore leans on 2020-2024 academic evidence rather than frontier recipes. Spoken evidence (2:30-3:20): pretraining is the base ('if we ignore pre-training and we just try to train our way to victory, we will get none of the things that we want'); post-training extracts the wanted behaviours 'out of this kind of primordial soup that is pre-training' with explicit data collection and steering, which is the framing behind the first misconception. Spoken evidence (5:42-6:45): algorithms are 'not really the secret sauce ... It's going to be the data'; the two-part recipe is narrated (demonstrations for SFT, then 'reinforcement learning of some kind'), and SFT is 'basically exactly the same as pre-training', the only real difference being the training data, which is why the SFT half of the lecture is almost entirely about data. Spoken evidence (3:28-5:37): the p5 caveat is expanded: Stiennon et al. and Anthropic HH have detailed annotation guidelines in their appendices, open recipes 'rely on distillation', and an anecdote from leaked Scale AI documents (annotators asked to out-write GPT-4 for Bard) illustrates the trade secrecy. The reward-model step is still not named aloud at this point (it is at 46:49).

misconceptions.belief: Post-training teaches the model new capabilities that pretraining lacked.
misconceptions.why_wrong: The deck's framing (p4, p27) is control over output, not new ability: pretraining data 'isn't quite what we want', and SFT works best when extracting behaviours already present. Capability comes from scale; post-training selects which behaviours surface.

misconceptions.belief: SFT and RLHF are alternative recipes; a lab picks one.
misconceptions.why_wrong: p6 and p31 present them as consecutive parts of one standard approach: imitation first, then reinforcement on top of the SFT model. Lecture 16's case studies (R1, Qwen 3) keep both stages.

predict.q: A lab has a strong pretrained model and wants it to answer in a helpful chat style. Per slide 6, in which order are the two post-training stages applied, and what does each stage consume?
predict.answer: First SFT (imitation) on demonstrations of the wanted behaviour, then RLHF (reinforcement) on pairwise preference data, starting from the SFT model.
predict.why: The standard approach is imitation followed by reinforcement: SFT gets the model to produce the right kind of output at all; RLHF then optimizes among such outputs using preferences.
predict.targets_misconception: SFT and RLHF are alternative recipes; a lab picks one.

transfer.q: A team pretrains on web text, then fine-tunes on 10k expert-written medical Q&A pairs and reports the model now 'knows medicine'. Using the lecture's p4/p27 framing, which of the three post-training questions does their claim skip, and what would the professor say the SFT most likely did instead?
transfer.answer: It skips 'how do we best make use of that data' / what SFT actually does: per p27 SFT mainly extracts pretraining behaviours (format, style of a medical answer) rather than adding knowledge; whatever medicine the model shows was largely already in the pretrained model.
transfer.why: Post-training is framed as tighter control over output, not as a knowledge source; fine-tuning on facts it does not know is what p20 warns causes hallucination.
transfer.varies: domain: medical knowledge instead of chat style; the claimed effect of SFT (knowledge) instead of behaviour
transfer.invariant: SFT is imitation of demonstrations; it selects among behaviours the pretrained model can already produce

choices: new calculus knowledge, learned from the 2,000 solutions
the answer format; the calculus was already in the model
nothing by itself; SFT only matters as a warm start for RLHF
check.answer: the answer format; the calculus was already in the model
check.why: p27: SFT works best when extracting pretraining behaviours, not adding new ones; small amounts of the right kind of data (style, instruction-following) make a big difference. 2,000 examples mostly teach presentation, which can lift a test score. SFT is a stage in its own right before RLHF (p6), not just a warm start.
check.varies: a score gain after a small SFT set on worked solutions, instead of a claim that medical Q&A taught medicine
check.invariant: SFT extracts and shapes behaviours the pretrained model already has
check.targets_misconception: Post-training teaches the model new capabilities that pretraining lacked.

knowledge_points.label: Open SFT data moved from NLP-benchmark style (FLAN) to chatty, detailed, then agentic/tool-use data
knowledge_points.statement: Open instruction datasets progressed FLAN -> Self-Instruct -> Alpaca -> ShareGPT/Vicuna -> OpenAssistant -> WizardLM -> Tulu 3 -> Nemotron, and the axes that changed are chattiness (FLAN is valid data but reads like an NLP benchmark; later sets give longer, more detailed responses), detail (OASST packs in factual knowledge and references) and tool use (recent SFT shifts toward agentic, tool-calling transcripts); less visible but important are scale and safety.

anchors.quote: FLAN Self-instruct Alpaca ShareGPT/Vicuna ... Open Assistant WizardLM Tulu3 Nemotron Tool use etc.
FLAN is (usually) valid data, but people don't want to talk to a NLP benchmark. Later datasets move towards longer, more detailed responses
Tool use – SFT in the last year or two has also been shifting much more towards tool/use, agentic downstream applications.
Length and bullet points (style variations) ... References, other complex knowledge ... Less visible, but important aspects.. ... Scale ... Safety
Nemotron-SFT-OpenCode-v1

the oldest and in some ways the most visionary of this is things like FLAN. ... NLP people have already collected a bunch of supervised data sets of inputs and outputs. ... Turned out, for various reasons, this was not the right thing to do.
the summaries are often hallucinated. ... the original NLP data sets, from which font was built, was not the highest of quality. ... really, the unnaturalness really gets you.

part of the theory of how post-training should work was that you needed scale. ... a lot of these data sets just get really much smaller, and it still works. ... it's the wrong point in some ways on the quality, quantity trade off.

why can't we use the model itself to generate data? ... The Berkeley folks had one called Vicuna in which they were using online user shared prompts ... It was a bunch of people getting together to write prompts and responses.
SFT data now, if you look at, for example Nemotron, so that's NVIDIA's open source efforts, their SFT data, a big chunk of it is these kinds of agentic SFT examples
people don't really want to talk to NLP benchmark, they want to talk to people. ... tool use and figuring out the right interface and API for all of this has been a big final shift

misconceptions.why_wrong: p14 says FLAN is '(usually) valid data'; the main problem is style and purpose: people do not want to converse with an NLP benchmark, so the target behaviour (chatty, detailed answers) is absent. Aloud (12:45-14:20) the professor names quality as one reason among three (the source datasets 'not the highest of quality', summaries 'often hallucinated'), alongside the unnatural templates and the wrong quality-versus-quantity trade-off, so cleaning the facts alone would still leave templated, terse targets.

misconceptions.belief: Every instruction dataset in the progression was written by humans.
misconceptions.why_wrong: Self-Instruct and Alpaca are model-generated (distilled), ShareGPT is scraped chats, OASST is crowd-written; the slide's lineage mixes sources, and p5 notes open-source post-training is 'lots of distillation'.

choices: Mostly wrong: FLAN labels are noisy, so the model hallucinates
Mostly right but terse and benchmark-like: it answers as if filling an NLP task template
Mostly right and chatty: FLAN already contains long multi-turn dialogue
predict.answer: Mostly right but terse and benchmark-like: it answers as if filling an NLP task template
predict.why: FLAN is valid data assembled from NLP benchmark templates (p10 examples: 'Write a subject line', 'OPTIONS: - World - Sports ...'); the model imitates that style. Later datasets move toward longer, more detailed responses because that is what people want to talk to.

transfer.q: A 2026 SFT set consists of transcripts where the assistant emits JSON tool_calls, reads a repo file and updates a todo list before answering (like slide 13). Which of the three p14 axes does this move along, and what new failure mode does it create that a chatty OASST-style set did not have?
transfer.answer: Tool use / agentic. New failure mode: the model must produce well-formed tool calls and act on their results, so errors are now format and action errors (malformed JSON, calling a tool that does not exist, ignoring the tool output), not only wrong or terse text.
transfer.why: The p9-p14 progression is defined by what behaviour the data demonstrates; agentic data demonstrates actions in an environment, so imitation errors are action errors.
transfer.varies: modality of the target behaviour: tool-calling transcripts instead of prose answers
transfer.invariant: SFT imitates whatever behaviour the dataset demonstrates, so the dataset's axis determines the model's failure modes

knowledge_points.label: Length is a confound in preference evaluation and an outcome of RLHF; benchmarks mostly ignore it
knowledge_points.statement: Models differ a lot in response length, and when quality is judged by preferences there are very strong length effects for both human and GPT-based judges, while these style factors are mostly irrelevant to other benchmark scores; RLHF then amplifies the confound because length effects are a very significant outcome of optimizing preferences.

anchors.quote: When evaluating by preferences, style matters. We see very strong length effects (in both humans and GPT-based evaluations)
Models vary a lot in response length..
These factors are (mostly) not that relevant for other benchmark perfs
Length effects are a very significant outcome of RLHF

anchors.ref: alpacafarm:§5 (length bias of human and simulated annotators)
singhal2024:§3 (length explains most of the reward gain)

anchors.quote: length is-- and style variation, in general, is a very, very big part of this post training process. ... All of these are conscious decisions that are made by the data collection folks.

when you go and evaluate preferences, these stylistic factors matter a ton. ... They will very often select responses that have bullet pointed lists in their outputs, or they will select responses that have more and longer detail.

it's very, very easy to fool yourself into thinking you're getting better data, when in reality, your models capabilities are not changing. ... you want to think about style control separately from capabilities control.

models are also very susceptible to the same kinds of biases as humans ... you could just push length of your responses way out. ... you can just RLHF on length alone, and you could do quite well on many of these benchmarks.

provenance.filtering_note: All four slides are plots: p16 ([Wang+ 2023]) response-length distributions per dataset, p17 ([Dubois+ 2023]) win rate vs length for human and GPT-4 judges, p18 a benchmark table, p48 ([Chen et al 2024], [Singhal et al 2024]) reward vs length under RLHF. None of the plotted numbers (win-rate deltas, token counts, correlation coefficients) survive in the text layer; the lecture gives no magnitude for 'very strong'. Length-controlled evaluation (AlpacaEval 2 LC) and length-normalized losses (p60) are the fixes the deck gestures at but does not explain. Spoken evidence (19:39-20:53): style and length are 'conscious decisions that are made by the data collection folks' (Claude's tone vs ChatGPT's chattiness); raters pick bullet-pointed and longer answers partly for a natural reason, since in a side-by-side setting 'more detailed and list like responses are generally good', but this distorts the chatbot's tone. Spoken evidence (21:07-21:58): the warning behind p18: with engagement signals 'it's very, very easy to fool yourself into thinking you're getting better data, when in reality, your models capabilities are not changing'; the AlpacaEval column moves while standard benchmarks do not, so 'think about style control separately from capabilities control'. Spoken evidence (1:04:30-1:05:23), p48 read aloud: models judging models are 'very susceptible to the same kinds of biases as humans ... even more problematic'; pushing response length out keeps raising model-judged win rates, with ChatGPT 3.5 the one outlier that is 'actually better', and one paper shows 'you can just RLHF on length alone' and do well on many benchmarks. Still no magnitude for 'very strong'.

misconceptions.belief: Using GPT-4 instead of humans as the preference judge removes the length bias.
misconceptions.why_wrong: p17 says the strong length effects appear in both human and GPT-based evaluations; the LM judge inherits (and p45 says agrees with) human preferences, bias included.

misconceptions.belief: If a model's length grows after RLHF, that is because longer answers are genuinely better.
misconceptions.why_wrong: p48 presents length growth as an outcome of the optimization itself: preferences reward length, so the policy learns length whether or not content improved. A length-controlled comparison is needed to tell.

predict.q: Model A and model B are identical except A was fine-tuned on data with 2x longer responses. You compare them with (i) GPT-4 pairwise preference and (ii) MMLU accuracy. Per slides 17-18, which comparison moves in A's favour and which barely moves?
predict.answer: The GPT-4 pairwise preference favours A (strong length effect, present in GPT-based judges too); MMLU barely moves (style factors are mostly not relevant to other benchmarks).
predict.why: Preference judgements reward style, including length, in both humans and LM judges; multiple-choice benchmarks score the answer token, so response style does not enter.
predict.targets_misconception: Using GPT-4 instead of humans as the preference judge removes the length bias.

transfer.q: After RLHF, a team reports its win rate against the SFT model rose from 50% to 65% and average response length doubled. Name the one additional comparison the lecture's p17/p48 evidence demands before crediting the gain to content, and say what result would undercut the claim.
transfer.answer: A length-controlled comparison (e.g. judge the RLHF model against SFT outputs of matched length, or a length-controlled win rate). If the advantage largely disappears at matched length, the gain was the length effect that RLHF is known to produce, not better content.
transfer.why: Length is simultaneously what the judge rewards (p17) and what RLHF learns to produce (p48), so an uncontrolled win rate confounds the two.
transfer.varies: functional: the question is about an RLHF outcome measured by win rate, not about dataset style
transfer.invariant: the judge's length preference is the same mechanism whether it is evaluating an SFT model or being optimized by RLHF

check.q: Two responses carry identical content, but one is padded to twice the length with restatements and extra bullet points. A GPT-4 pairwise judge compares them many times. Relative to 50%, which way does the padded response's win rate move? Start with up, down or same.
check.answer: Up: preference judges, GPT-based ones included, show strong length effects, so the padded version wins more often despite adding nothing.
check.why: p17: when evaluating by preferences there are very strong length effects in both human and GPT-based evaluations; content is held fixed here, so the deviation from 50% is the length effect itself.
check.varies: content is held fixed and only length changes, instead of a post-RLHF win rate with length confounded
check.invariant: preference judgements, human or GPT-4, are biased toward longer responses
check.targets_misconception: Using GPT-4 instead of humans as the preference judge removes the length bias.

knowledge_points.label: Fine-tuning on facts the model does not know teaches it to hallucinate
knowledge_points.statement: An SFT example that cites a specific paper can teach either the fact (Bivens & Mishel 2013) or the behaviour (emit citations when asked); folklore backed by Gekhman et al. says that fine-tuning on facts the model does not already know makes it hallucinate, because the gradient rewards producing confident citation-shaped text regardless of grounding, so you may not want to fine-tune on tail knowledge even when tail knowledge is the use case, and RL-style correctness feedback is the principled alternative.

anchors.quote: Folklore: Fine-tuning a model on 'facts it doesn't know' makes it hallucinate

What is this example teaching the model? 1. Teaching the model about Bivens J & Mishel, L 2. Teaching the model to output citations when asked to do so (But by what mechanism? Does the model know about cites?)

You may not want to fine-tune on tail knowledge, even that's the LM use case ... In principle, 'RL' style correctness feedback could help ... Knowledge storage and extraction in LMs is messy, and nuanced.

anchors.ref: gekhman2024:§4 (Unknown examples fit slowly and raise hallucination)

anchors.quote: this is actually teaching the model two different things at once. ... it will misgeneralize, and it will hallucinate out a reference instead of actually giving a proper reference.

the Folklore, which I think is not wrong. ... if you train a model, especially at the SFT phase, to emit facts that it does not, this will make it hallucinate. ... Whereas if you're training on only known facts, you don't necessarily see this.
you might not want to train on the highest quality data if the model doesn't already that data. ... especially if it's associated with markers like reference colon.

So in some ways, SFT isn't doing the wrong thing. This is a correct sequence. The problem is SFT is the generalization properties of this. ... if I generalize based on the template, I'm in big trouble.
the length of a Wikipedia article, for example, might be a proxy for its well-knownness. ... knowledge itself can't really be pinned down, precisely.

provenance.filtering_note: p20's two panels ([Schulman 2023], [Gekhman 2023]) are images; the Gekhman result that Unknown examples are fit slowly and that their fitting correlates with rising hallucination on held-out questions is not in the text layer, and the slide mis-dates the paper (arXiv 2024). The mechanism ('by what mechanism?') is posed as a question, not answered: the supervised loss cannot distinguish a grounded citation from a plausible-looking one, so it reinforces the surface form. 'RL style correctness feedback' is left as 'in principle'; the deck does not say how to verify correctness at scale (lecture 16's verifiable rewards are the follow-up). Correction from the audio: the note said the mechanism ('by what mechanism?') is 'posed as a question, not answered'. Aloud it is answered (22:30-24:01): one example teaches two things at once, the knowledge and the format, and teaching the format with a piece of unknown knowledge is 'teaching the model to forcibly emit unknown knowledge'; the model 'will hallucinate out a reference', since models 'don't really know necessarily whether a reference is true or false'. The Q&A (27:34-28:12) refines this: the SFT loss 'isn't doing the wrong thing' (the reference is a correct sequence); the problem is that SFT may generalize from the template rather than the content. The note's 'gradient rewards confident citation-shaped text' is consistent with this. Spoken evidence (24:01-24:18): the Gekhman-style result is said aloud: training on unknown facts leads to hallucination and overfitting, 'Whereas if you're training on only known facts, you don't necessarily see this'. Spoken evidence (24:18-25:26): Schulman's argument is relayed and endorsed ('the argument is sound'): teaching what the model knows has to be policy-dependent, so RL is useful 'for things that are model-dependent, knowing what you know'; the Q&A at 26:20 gives the mechanism (see rl-reads-internal-knowledge-signal). Spoken evidence (25:47-26:18): 'tail knowledge' has no formal definition; the length of a Wikipedia article is one proxy for well-knownness used in his past work.

misconceptions.belief: Adding more factually correct SFT examples can only make a model more factual.
misconceptions.why_wrong: p27 point 2 and p20: correct facts the model has not stored are 'facts it doesn't know'; fitting them teaches the model to produce confident fact-shaped text without grounding, which generalizes as hallucination.

misconceptions.belief: The citation in the monopsony example teaches the model about Bivens and Mishel.
misconceptions.why_wrong: p19's alternative (2) is what the professor favours: one example mostly teaches the behaviour 'output a citation when asked'; whether the model knows that reference is a separate question about pretraining knowledge.

predict.q: You fine-tune on 5,000 QA pairs about obscure 2025 local-election results that the base model has never seen, all verified correct. Per slide 20, what happens to the model's hallucination rate on unrelated factual questions?
choices: It falls: the model has learned more true facts
It rises: the model learns to produce confident answers it cannot ground
It is unchanged: SFT only affects the fine-tuned topics
predict.answer: It rises: the model learns to produce confident answers it cannot ground
predict.why: These are 'facts it doesn't know'. The supervised loss rewards emitting specific-sounding answers regardless of whether the model has the knowledge, and that behaviour transfers to other questions.
predict.targets_misconception: Adding more factually correct SFT examples can only make a model more factual.
predict.distractor_from: option 1: 'correct data can only help'; option 3: 'SFT effects stay local to the topic'

transfer.q: Instead of fine-tuning on the unknown election facts, a team gives the model retrieval access and fine-tunes on examples where the answer is copied from a retrieved document. Using the p19 distinction, say which of the two things (fact vs behaviour) this SFT now teaches and why the p20 hallucination mechanism is weakened.
transfer.answer: It teaches the behaviour 'answer from the retrieved text', not the facts themselves; the facts are supplied at inference, so the model is no longer being trained to produce specifics it cannot ground, which is what drove hallucination.
transfer.why: The hallucination mechanism needs a gap between what the target asserts and what the model can know; grounding the target in context closes that gap while keeping the behaviour-teaching role of SFT.
transfer.varies: functional: the SFT target is grounded in retrieved context instead of in parametric knowledge
transfer.invariant: SFT teaches the behaviour exhibited by the targets; hallucination arises only when targets assert knowledge the model lacks

check.q: A team must pick one SFT set to add to a model. Per slides 19-20, which is most likely to raise its hallucination rate on unrelated factual questions?
choices: 2,000 correct QA pairs on facts the base model already knows
2,000 correct QA pairs on facts the base model has never seen
2,000 QA pairs whose answers are copied from a provided passage
none of them, since every answer in all three is correct
check.answer: 2,000 correct QA pairs on facts the base model has never seen
check.why: p20 (Gekhman et al.): fine-tuning on facts the model does not know makes it hallucinate, because it is trained to produce specifics it cannot ground. Known facts only reinforce existing knowledge, and copying from a passage teaches a grounded behaviour.
check.varies: the learner chooses among three SFT sets rather than analysing a retrieval redesign
check.invariant: SFT on unknown facts trains ungrounded confident answering; grounded or known content does not
check.targets_misconception: Adding more factually correct SFT examples can only make a model more factual.
distractor_from: '2,000 correct QA pairs on facts the base model already knows' <- plausible: assumes any factual SFT is equally risky
'2,000 QA pairs whose answers are copied from a provided passage' <- plausible: treats the copied answers as new facts rather than a grounded behaviour
'none of them, since every answer in all three is correct' <- misconception: 'Adding more factually correct SFT examples can only make a model more factual.'

retrieval.answer: Fine-tuning a model on facts it doesn't know makes it hallucinate.

knowledge_points.label: RL can curb hallucination only by reading an internal 'I know' signal; it cannot create one
knowledge_points.statement: An SFT reference forces the citation format whatever the model knows, but RL rewards the model's own outputs, so if its activations already separate facts it knows from facts it does not, RL can learn to emit a reference only when that 'I know' signal is on; if the model has no internal signal of what it knows, RL cannot supply one. This is the lecture's folk account of why 'RL style correctness feedback could help' (p21): teaching a model what it knows has to be policy-dependent.

anchors.quote: Imagine, the model has internal to it. I know something direction inside it's activations. ... when you RL, you might notice that you get good rewards when you generate references in the I know stuff direction. ... If you don't know what you know at all, at any level, RL cannot help you there.

John Schulman makes a separate argument, which is that this is the reason why you need reinforcement learning ... You can't have an external person shoving knowledge down your throat if you want the model to be calibrated about what it knows and doesn't.
For things that are model-dependent, knowing what you know, RL is a very useful way to teach models to not say things that it does not know.
In principle, 'RL' style correctness feedback could help

provenance.filtering_note: Spoken only for the mechanism and its limit. p21 says only 'In principle, 'RL' style correctness feedback could help', and sft-tail-knowledge-hallucination records that the deck does not say how. Aloud, Schulman's argument is relayed and called sound (24:18-24:48): calibration about what a model knows has to be 'policy-dependent', since 'You can't have an external person shoving knowledge down your throat'. Asked in Q&A why RL would help with hallucination (26:20), the professor gives what he calls 'a folk story' (26:31-27:21): suppose the activations hold an 'I know something' direction; SFT forced references regardless, but under RL references produced in the 'I know' direction earn good rewards and those in the 'I don't know' direction bad ones, so the policy learns to condition citing on the signal. 'If you don't know what you know at all, at any level, RL cannot help you there.' No experiment is given. The probe accuracies in the prompts are the author's illustration of 'an internal signal', not the lecture's. The follow-up Q&A (27:28-28:12) adds that SFT's loss is not wrong (the reference is a correct sequence); the trouble is whether SFT generalizes the template or the fact. Lecture 16 (verifiable rewards) makes correctness rewards concrete.

prerequisites.note: Given in Q&A right after the tail-knowledge takeaways (26:20).

misconceptions.belief: RL with a correctness reward can stop any model from hallucinating, whatever it represents internally.
misconceptions.why_wrong: RL can only route a signal the model already has into its outputs. 'If you don't know what you know at all, at any level, RL cannot help you there' (27:16): with no internal known/unknown distinction, nothing the policy can condition on predicts the reward, so citing cannot become selective.

misconceptions.belief: SFT on carefully verified references teaches a model when to cite as well as RL does.
misconceptions.why_wrong: An SFT reference is written by someone else and is the same for every model, so it cannot depend on what this model knows; by Schulman's argument (24:33-24:48) 'cite only what you know' has to come from the model's own outputs being rewarded or penalized. A verified reference is a known fact for one model and an unknown one for another.

predict.q: After SFT on many answers ending in 'References:', a model fabricates citations on obscure topics. A linear probe on its activations predicts whether it can answer a question correctly no better than chance (51%). You run RL that rewards real citations and penalizes fabricated ones. Per the lecture's folk story, can RL make this model cite only when it knows? Why or why not?
predict.answer: No. RL can only teach the policy to condition citing on an internal 'I know' signal, and this model has none (the probe is at chance). At best RL suppresses citations across the board, real ones included; it cannot make them selective.
predict.why: 'If you don't know what you know at all, at any level, RL cannot help you there' (27:16). The reward attaches to whatever the policy can condition on; with no known/unknown distinction inside the model, there is nothing to attach the 'cite here, not there' decision to.
predict.targets_misconception: RL with a correctness reward can stop any model from hallucinating, whatever it represents internally.

transfer.q: A code model invents library functions that do not exist. A probe shows its activations separate APIs it has seen often from ones it has not, at 90% accuracy. Team A adds 5,000 SFT examples of correct calls to rare APIs; team B runs RL that rewards code that runs and penalizes calls to non-existent functions. Which team should expect fewer invented functions on rare APIs it has not trained on, and why?
transfer.answer: Team B. The model has an internal 'I know this API' signal, so RL can teach it to call a function only when the signal is on (and otherwise hedge or look it up). Team A's SFT forces the call format on APIs the model may not know, which the lecture says induces hallucination.
transfer.why: RL rewards the model's own outputs and so can extract an existing knowledge signal into the policy; SFT on tail facts teaches the format whatever the model knows (sft-tail-knowledge-hallucination). The probe result is what makes RL's route available here.
transfer.targets_misconception: SFT on carefully verified references teaches a model when to cite as well as RL does.
transfer.varies: domain (code APIs instead of citations) and a head-to-head of SFT vs RL when a knowledge signal exists
transfer.invariant: RL can turn an existing internal knowledge signal into selective behaviour; SFT on unknown facts forces the format regardless

check.q: Two models get the same RL run, which rewards real citations and penalizes fabricated ones. In model A, a probe reads 'knows the answer' from activations at 92% accuracy; in model B at 51% (chance). By the lecture's account, in which model can RL make citing selective, so that it cites mainly when it knows?
choices: model A, whose activations separate known from unknown
both, because the two models get the same reward
model B, because it has more fabrications to fix
check.answer: model A, whose activations separate known from unknown
distractor_from: 'both, because the two models get the same reward' <- misconception: 'RL with a correctness reward can stop any model from hallucinating, whatever it represents internally.'
'model B, because it has more fabrications to fix' <- plausible error: more errors means more reward signal, ignoring that the policy needs an internal signal to condition on
check.why: RL can only extract a known/unknown signal that is already in the activations (26:39-27:16). Model A has one; model B's probe is at chance, so the same reward cannot make its citing selective.
check.varies: a comparison of two models under one reward, instead of one model's outcome
check.invariant: RL needs an internal 'I know' signal to make behaviour depend on knowledge
check.targets_misconception: RL with a correctness reward can stop any model from hallucinating, whatever it represents internally.

retrieval.q: In the lecture's folk story, what must a model already have for RL to reduce its hallucinated references?
retrieval.answer: An internal representation of what it knows (an 'I know' vs 'I don't know' direction in its activations) that the policy can learn to condition on.

retrieval.q: What is Schulman's argument, as the professor relays it, for why SFT alone cannot teach a model what it knows?
retrieval.answer: Knowing what you know is policy-dependent: demonstrations written by someone else are the same whatever the model knows, so calibration has to come from rewarding the model's own outputs.

knowledge_points.label: Safety tuning trades the violation rate against the false-refusal rate
knowledge_points.statement: Safety tuning balances two error rates: the violation rate (harmful requests that get answered) and the false-refusal rate (benign requests that get refused, such as 'how do I kill a Python process'); the goal is a good Pareto trade-off between them, so safety data is tailored to navigate the trade-off, and driving the violation rate down by refusing more is not success on its own.

anchors.quote: the framework by which all the safety tuning approaches operate is to balance two things. ... how often am I allowing bad queries to get through, which is, I think the violation rate here. ... you also want to not over refuse because someone might ask a question like, how do I kill a Python process.

And so the false refusal rate also needs to be low. So want to control this and have a good Pareto trade between the two. ... you basically create various kinds of tailored data to navigate this trade off.

filter out a whole bunch unsafe behaviors that were being attempted to be done on these chat interfaces, as well as jailbreaks ... created essentially the preferred response, which is to resist the jailbreak in one case, and to say no in another case.
Main safety approach – extract scenarios from users

provenance.filtering_note: Spoken only. The safety slides (p23-p25) are screenshots whose text layer keeps only 'Details are pretty sparse', '# Examples? ~ few thousand in Llama 2', 'Pipeline with most details' and 'extract scenarios from users'. Neither metric is in the text layer, but p23's image plots exactly these two: the Llama 3 report's Figure 18, violation rate (%) against false refusal rate (%) for Llama 3 8B and 70B across safety/helpfulness mixes (violation falls from ~70% to ~12-20% as false refusal rises from ~1.7% to ~3%; 8B needs a higher share of safety data than 70B), and its excerpt introduces 'borderline prompts' to cut false refusals. Aloud (29:31-30:11), every safety-tuning approach balances the violation rate ('how often am I allowing bad queries to get through') against the false-refusal rate, with 'how do I kill a Python process' as the over-refusal example, aiming for 'a good Pareto trade between the two' with tailored data. The Tulu 3 / OLMo recipe (30:32-31:50) mines unsafe requests and jailbreak attempts from WildChat logs and writes the preferred response (resist the jailbreak, or say no), about '50,000-ish' examples (spoken number, not cross-checked); closed labs similarly mine usage logs and 'play whack-a-mole' (31:53-32:13). That benign look-alike prompts with helpful answers are the usual lever against false refusals is the author's reading of 'tailored data'; the professor does not name it. The rates in the prompts are the author's. small-data-big-behavior-change's p26 result (about 500 examples) concerns the violation side.

prerequisites.note: Safety is introduced as a post-training responsibility (28:16), after the SFT data discussion.

misconceptions.belief: The best safety-tuned model is the one with the lowest violation rate.
misconceptions.why_wrong: The violation rate is half the objective. A model that refuses 'how do I kill a Python process' has a low violation rate and a high false-refusal rate; the lecture's target is a good Pareto trade-off between the two (29:58).

misconceptions.belief: Safety data only needs malicious prompts paired with refusals.
misconceptions.why_wrong: Refusal-only data pushes the violation rate down and the false-refusal rate up. The data has to be 'tailored ... to navigate this trade off' (30:04), so both sides are covered.

predict.q: A team safety-tunes a chatbot on 20,000 malicious prompts paired with refusals, and nothing else. Its violation rate drops from 12% to 1%. Name the second quantity the lecture says safety tuning must track, and predict which way it moves.
predict.answer: The false-refusal rate, which likely rises: with only refusals in the data, benign requests that look risky (like 'how do I kill a Python process') get refused too.
predict.why: Safety tuning trades the violation rate against the false-refusal rate (29:31-30:04). Refusal-only data moves along the trade-off toward refusing more; it does not improve both.
predict.targets_misconception: Safety data only needs malicious prompts paired with refusals.

transfer.q: Three safety-tuned models: X has a 2% violation rate and a 25% false-refusal rate; Y has 4% and 3%; Z has 5% and 6%. Which model is dominated, and does picking the lowest violation rate give the best deployment candidate?
transfer.answer: Z is dominated by Y, which is better on both rates. The lowest violation rate picks X, which refuses a quarter of benign requests; X versus Y is a choice of point on the Pareto trade-off, and Y is the more balanced point.
transfer.why: The lecture judges safety tuning on both rates together ('a good Pareto trade between the two', 29:58), so a single-number ranking by violation rate ignores half the objective.
transfer.targets_misconception: The best safety-tuned model is the one with the lowest violation rate.
transfer.varies: a comparison of three models on both rates, instead of one model's change after tuning
transfer.invariant: safety is judged on the pair (violation rate, false-refusal rate), not on violations alone

check.q: A safety-tuned assistant answers 'How do I kill a zombie process on Linux?' with 'Sorry, I can't help with killing anything.' In the lecture's framework, which rate does this response count toward?
choices: the false-refusal rate
the violation rate
neither; refusing is the safe default
distractor_from: 'the violation rate' <- confusion of the two error types
'neither; refusing is the safe default' <- misconception: 'The best safety-tuned model is the one with the lowest violation rate.'
check.why: The request is benign (process management), so refusing it is a false refusal, the error the professor illustrates with 'how do I kill a Python process' (29:45). A violation would be answering a harmful request.
check.varies: a single response to classify, instead of rates to compare
check.invariant: refusing a benign request is an error (false refusal), not a free safety margin
check.targets_misconception: The best safety-tuned model is the one with the lowest violation rate.

retrieval.q: Which two rates does every safety-tuning approach balance, according to the lecture?
retrieval.answer: The violation rate (bad queries that get through) and the false-refusal rate (benign queries that get refused).

retrieval.q: Where did the Tulu 3 / OLMo pipeline get the prompts for its safety SFT data?
retrieval.answer: From WildChat usage logs: unsafe requests and jailbreak attempts mined at scale, each given a preferred response (resist the jailbreak, or refuse).

knowledge_points.label: Hundreds of examples of the right behaviour move safety and style; the long tail still needs more data
knowledge_points.statement: Because SFT extracts behaviours the pretrained model already has rather than adding new ones, small amounts of the right kind of data (safety, instruction-following, style) make a big difference: ~500 safety samples give significant safety improvements and adding 500 Alpaca-style safety examples makes models follow safety guidelines, while Llama 2 used only a few thousand; but adding factually correct data can sometimes hurt, and there is a long tail of behaviours that benefits from more data.

anchors.quote: Significant improvements to safety with ~500 samples. ... Adding 500 Alpaca-style examples makes models follow safety guidelines
Instruction fine-tuning (SFT) works works best when we are just extracting pre- training behaviors, not adding new ones

Adding (factually correct!) data can sometimes hurt ... Small amounts of the right kinds of behavior (safety, instruction-following, style) make a big difference, but there is a long-tail that benefits from more data
# Examples? ~ few thousand in Llama 2

if you have a sufficiently capable model, it does not take very many examples to steer these systems. ... even with as little as 500 examples, the rate at which you follow malicious instructions or other kinds of hate speech instructions, and so on, drops dramatically.

models already have am I going to be a safe model or an unsafe model access inside of it after pre-training ... you want to enforce really fine grained distinctions about what is safe and not safe, you do need very large scale data collection
if you're extracting pre-training behaviors, like it's already in there somewhere in pre-training ... adding data or factually correct ones can sometimes hurt you, at least in terms of hallucination.
you usually have something like a few thousand or tens of thousands of examples. ... in Llama 2, I think it's about a few thousand examples that are used for this process.
we don't really know per se. We can know what things aren't in pre-training. ... We can't show necessarily that, for example, safety is something that's in pre-training per se.

provenance.filtering_note: p26's two plots ('(Hate speech)', '(Anthropic HH)') are images; the harmfulness scores at 0/100/300/500/1000/2000 added safety examples, and the slide's implicit observation that too many safety examples make the model over-refuse, are not in the text layer. The paper behind p26 (Bianchi et al.) is not named on the slide (inference). p22-p25 (misinformation and scams motivation, 'Details are pretty sparse', the Llama 2 pipeline screenshots, 'extract scenarios from users') are context. The deck never names LIMA ('less is more for alignment'); the LIMA-style claim is stated as point 3 of p27 and supported by the safety result, Alpaca's small distilled set and the agentic-SFT trend, with the explicit hedge about the long tail. No number is given for 'the long tail'. Spoken evidence (32:14-33:07): the p26 plots are read aloud: with 'as little as 500 examples' of refusals, compliance with malicious and hate-speech instructions 'drops dramatically', a 'very small push' that gives an across-the-board reduction, because models already have a safe/unsafe axis after pretraining. Spoken evidence (33:21-33:40): the 'long tail' is given a concrete meaning: a lab that wants 'really fine grained distinctions about what is safe and not safe' still needs 'very large scale data collection'. Spoken evidence (34:06): 'factually correct can hurt' is tied to hallucination (sft-tail-knowledge-hallucination). Spoken evidence (34:33-34:57, Q&A): whether a behaviour is 'already in pre-training' cannot be checked directly; one can show what is not there (generalization to very rare programming languages is hard with SFT) but not that safety is, so 'extracting' is a working hypothesis. Spoken evidence (30:11-31:05): safety sets are 'a few thousand or tens of thousands of examples'; Llama 2 'about a few thousand' (matching p23), although he also says the Llama 2 report does not 'even talk about how many examples' (29:25); Tulu 3 / OLMo's safety component is 'something like 50,000-ish examples' (spoken number, not cross-checked). Correction from the audio: the note calls p22-p25 'the Llama 2 pipeline screenshots'. Aloud only p23 is Llama 2; p24 ('Pipeline with most details') is Ai2's Tulu 3 post-training pipeline for OLMo ('two or three' in the captions, 30:32-30:57), and p25's 'extract scenarios from users' is its WildChat mining (31:12-31:50). The note also says the over-refusal side of p26 is not in the text layer: that is still true, but the trade-off is said aloud in general terms (29:31-30:11, safety-violation-vs-false-refusal). Slide image audit (p23): the screenshot is from the Llama 3 report (its Figure 18, legend 'Llama 3 8B / 70B', plus the 'Finetuning data' paragraph on borderline prompts and synthetic adversarial data); only the slide's corner annotation '# Examples? ~ few thousand in Llama 2' is about Llama 2. So the few-thousand figure is the slide's claim about Llama 2, while calling the screenshot 'Llama 2' (29:18) is a slip.

misconceptions.belief: Because 500 examples suffice for safety, a few hundred examples suffice for any post-training goal.
misconceptions.why_wrong: p27 limits the claim to 'the right kinds of behavior' (safety, instruction-following, style) that the pretrained model can already produce, and adds 'there is a long-tail that benefits from more data'; p28-p30 then introduce mid-training precisely to scale instruction data up.

misconceptions.belief: More SFT data is monotonically better, so safety data should be maximized.
misconceptions.why_wrong: p27 point 2 says adding (even factually correct) data can hurt, and the p26 plots (image) show the harm/helpfulness trade-off saturating; quality and kind of behaviour, not count, is the lever.

predict.q: A team has a 7B instruction-tuned model that answers harmful requests. Per slide 26, roughly how many safety demonstrations do they need to add for a significant improvement: tens, hundreds, or hundreds of thousands?
choices: Tens
Hundreds (about 500)
Hundreds of thousands
predict.answer: Hundreds (about 500)

transfer.q: The same team now wants the model to answer questions about a proprietary 2,000-page internal API that never appeared in pretraining, and proposes 500 SFT examples 'because 500 worked for safety'. Using p27, say why the analogy fails and which of p27's two caveats applies.
transfer.answer: Safety was extracting an existing behaviour; the API facts are new knowledge the model lacks. p27's 'adding (factually correct) data can sometimes hurt' and the 'long tail benefits from more data' caveats apply: 500 examples will not install the knowledge and may teach confident hallucination instead.
transfer.why: The small-data rule depends on the behaviour already being in the pretrained model; it does not transfer to adding knowledge.
transfer.varies: functional: the goal switches from selecting a behaviour (refusal) to installing knowledge (API facts)
transfer.invariant: SFT's sample efficiency comes from extraction; both caveats of p27 are about data that must add something new

knowledge_points.label: Mid-training: mix instruction data into the end of pretraining, then a short SFT, to scale SFT without forgetting
knowledge_points.statement: When you have the compute and data to scale instruction tuning far beyond 'just do gradient descent', the increasingly popular two-phase recipe is: (1) pretrain on web data, (2) mix instruction-tuning data into pretraining, (3) run an actual but short instruction-tuning round; this lets instruction data scale up without catastrophic forgetting, is common knowledge among LLM companies but undocumented, and was publicized by MiniCPM and JetMoE.

anchors.quote: 1. Pre-train on web/pretraining data 2. Mix in instruction-tuning data into pre-training 3. Do an actual (but short) instruction-tuning round.
Lets you scale up instruction tuning w/o catastrophic forgetting
The recipe is common knowledge among many LLM companies (but not documented) ... Publicized in recent Chinese-derived LMs (miniCPM, jetMoE)
Just do gradient descent.. ... You have tons of compute and data, you want to scale up instruction tuning

anchors.ref: minicpm:§3.3 (decay stage with high-quality SFT data mixed in)

anchors.quote: this increasing trend of turning instruction tuning into part of pre-training. ... instruction tuning data, is now getting mixed in at the tail end of training when the decay phase usually of training happens. ... this really allows you to scale up instruction tuning.
when someone tells you something is a base model, that's kind of a lie. ... base models today are pre-trained on ultra chat, and who knows what else.
I think this one's from MiniCPM. ... you're kind of switching to this higher quality, and also very chatty data set. ... So almost everyone does this today.
No, this is pure pre-training. And so you're also predicting the prompt as well.

misconceptions.belief: Scaling SFT is just running more steps of the same post-training fine-tune.
misconceptions.why_wrong: p28-p29 say that in academic settings 'just do gradient descent' is it, but at scale a long late fine-tune on narrow data causes catastrophic forgetting, which is why the data is mixed into pretraining instead.

predict.q: A lab has 50B tokens of instruction data and tries to use all of it in a post-pretraining SFT stage. Per slide 29, what problem does the professor expect, and what is the recipe's fix?
predict.answer: Catastrophic forgetting of pretraining abilities. Fix: mix the instruction data into pretraining (phase 2), then run only a short instruction-tuning round at the end.
predict.why: A long fine-tune on a narrow distribution overwrites what pretraining learned; seeing the instruction data alongside web data during pretraining lets it scale without that loss.
predict.targets_misconception: Scaling SFT is just running more steps of the same post-training fine-tune.

knowledge_points.label: The decay phase gets the best data and is the cheap bench for data-mix ablations
knowledge_points.statement: The highest-quality data goes into the decay (mid-training) phase, because it is the part of pre-training closest to deployment and runs at the lowest learning rate; and because the decay is much shorter than pre-training (something like ten decay runs per full run), data-mix ablations are run on it and their results are carried back to set the pre-training mix. Pre-training as a whole cannot be made high quality because there are not enough high-quality tokens.

anchors.quote: Usually, the intuition is you want the reverse, that the decay is the most important part of your training. It's the part that's closest to deployment during pre-training. Also, it's the part where the lowest learning rate.
midtraining is much shorter than full pre-training. ... you can run something like 10 of these for each one of these
in the decay phase, you do a lot of data ablations, which are cheap to run ... So to decide the pre-training mix, often, you actually run a bunch of ablations on decay.
The reason why you don't just make pre-training high quality is you just don't have enough tokens.
2. Mix in instruction-tuning data into pre-training

transfer.q: Your team must place two datasets: 3T tokens of filtered web text and 40B tokens of curated textbooks and Q&A. One colleague proposes training on the 40B curated tokens only, 'since quality is what matters'. Another proposes the curated data first and the web text last. Using the lecture's reasoning, what do you do instead, and why?
transfer.answer: Pre-train on the web text and concentrate the curated data in the decay phase at the end. Curated-only runs out of tokens (40B is far too little for a full run); curated-first wastes it, because the decay is the phase closest to deployment and at the lowest learning rate.
transfer.why: Both of the professor's reasons (38:56-39:11) point the best data to the decay, and 'you just don't have enough tokens' (40:51) rules out making all of pre-training high quality.
transfer.targets_misconception: Lower-quality data belongs at the end of training, where the small learning rate limits its damage.

retrieval.answer: The decay is much shorter (something like 10 decay runs per full run), so ablations are cheap; and there are not enough high-quality tokens to fill a whole pre-training run.

knowledge_points.label: SFT fits a reference distribution; RLHF maximizes a measurable reward, treating the LM as a policy
knowledge_points.statement: Imitation (SFT) fits p_hat(y|x) to a reference distribution p*(y|x), a pure generative-modelling view that requires samples from the reference policy; optimization (RLHF) instead finds the p that maximizes E_p[R(y,x)] for a reward you can measure, treating the LM as a policy rather than a model of a distribution; the reason to optimize is the generation-validation gap: people do not always write the thing they prefer in LM outputs.

anchors.quote: Pure generative modeling perspective ... Requires samples from reference policy
Maximize some reward function that we can measure ... LMs are policies, not a model of some distribution
Why optimize? G-V gap ... People don't always write the thing that they prefer in LM outputs..

anchors.ref: zhang2023:§5 (LM summaries preferred over reference summaries)

anchors.quote: in pre-training, what are we doing? ... This is purely a generative modeling problem. ... we are no longer playing a fit a distribution game. We are fitting a maximize a reward game.
I can totally collapse out my distribution onto a single point for every input. ... And that would be OK, as long as it got a good reward.

there is sometimes a big difference in what they say they want and what they generate. ... a few annotators actually preferred Instruct Davinci, which was the predecessor to ChatGPT, over their own writing.
because of this gap, sometimes you might want to rate outputs rather than just to generate demonstrations. ... verifying a proof is probably much easier than generating the proof.
SFT is this dense feature supervision, whereas RL is the self-taught policy supervision. ... you're getting your own output from your own policy.

provenance.filtering_note: The two objectives on p32 (and its repeat p50) are set in math glyphs whose text layer is garbled (the hat on p and the subscript p survive only as symbols), so the formulas are restated in words in the statement rather than quoted. p33's G-V gap evidence is an image from Zhang et al. 2023 (annotators prefer LM summaries to the human-written references): no numbers survive. 'G-V' is not expanded on the slide; 'generation-validation' is the author's expansion. The slide does not say that RLHF also requires samples (from the current policy); the contrast is about whose samples: the reference distribution's for SFT vs the policy's own for RLHF. Spoken evidence (42:23-43:56): the p32 contrast is called 'quite important': pre-training and SFT are 'purely a generative modeling problem', RLHF is 'a maximize a reward game', and a policy 'can totally collapse out my distribution onto a single point for every input ... as long as it got a good reward' (the root of mode-collapse-calibration). Spoken evidence (44:14-45:18): the p33 G-V evidence is narrated: freelance writers asked to summarize news, some of whom preferred Instruct Davinci's summaries to their own and, interviewed, said 'actually, this is pretty good stuff'; 'people aren't really these optimal systems', so rating outputs can beat collecting demonstrations. Spoken evidence (45:25-45:46): a second reason the slide lacks: in some domains 'verification is a lot easier than generation' (math proofs; DeepSeek's self-verification), deferred to the next lecture. Together the two reasons support the note's 'generation-validation' expansion of 'G-V'. Spoken evidence (35:12-35:51, Q&A, earlier in the talk): 'the lines are very blurry' between SFT and RL (expert iteration 'look[s] like SFT with extra bells and whistles'); the distinction is the feedback: SFT is dense supervision, RL is 'self-taught policy supervision' on 'your own output from your own policy', so the policy may not drift as far. This is the 'whose samples' point the note makes.

misconceptions.belief: RLHF is just SFT on better data; both fit the model to examples of good outputs.
misconceptions.why_wrong: p32: SFT fits a distribution and needs samples from the reference; RLHF maximizes expected reward over the policy's own outputs. The RLHF objective has no reference distribution to imitate, only a reward to climb.

misconceptions.belief: If humans can judge which output is better, they could just write the better output and we could SFT on it.
misconceptions.why_wrong: p33's G-V gap: people do not always write what they prefer, so the preference signal contains information that demonstrations do not; optimizing against the judgement reaches outputs no demonstrator wrote.

predict.q: Human annotators consistently prefer a model's summaries over the human-written reference summaries in the training set. Per slides 32-33, what is the ceiling on an SFT model trained on those references, and why does RLHF escape it?
predict.answer: SFT can at best reproduce the reference distribution, which annotators like less than the model's outputs; RLHF maximizes the preference reward directly, so it can move to outputs people prefer but did not write (the G-V gap).
predict.why: Imitation is bounded by the demonstrations; optimization is bounded only by what the reward can measure.
predict.targets_misconception: If humans can judge which output is better, they could just write the better output and we could SFT on it.

transfer.q: A chess engine is trained two ways: (A) predict the next move of grandmaster games; (B) maximize win rate by playing itself. Map A and B onto p32's two columns and name the p32 requirement that A has and B does not.
transfer.answer: A is imitation (fit the grandmaster distribution; requires samples from the reference policy, i.e. grandmaster games); B is optimization (maximize a measurable reward, the win; the engine is a policy). B needs no reference samples, only the reward.
transfer.why: The distinction is about the training signal: samples of a target distribution versus a measurable reward on the policy's own actions.
transfer.varies: domain: chess instead of language, win instead of preference
transfer.invariant: imitation needs reference samples and is bounded by them; optimization needs only a measurable reward on the policy's own outputs

knowledge_points.label: RLHF data is pairwise comparisons from crowd or expert annotators; quality control is the hard part
knowledge_points.statement: The standard RLHF data setup is pairwise feedback: an annotator sees two model outputs for one prompt and marks the better one under a guideline (InstructGPT's is the canonical example); collecting it through platforms (Outlier, ScaleAI) is hard because high-quality verifiable annotators are scarce, annotators rarely check correctness, AI use must be policed, compensation varies widely, and the market is shifting toward expert annotation, with ethical issues at scale.

anchors.quote: Standard 'pairwise feedback' setup
Hard to get really high-quality, verifiable annotators ... Hard to get them to really check correctness ... Have to be careful about AI use..
Large variation in compensation ... Lots of growth in "expert annotation"
Caveat: many platforms, covers only one (Outlier, ScaleAI)
Data collection at scale can have significant issues
RLHF data collection is (also) hard! Many confounding factors
the general way in which we do this is to get pairwise ratings. ... you're going to give a response saying response one or two is better.
at least in the InstructGPT case, they say, OK, we want you to rate these outputs for being helpful, truthful, and harmless.
actually, their rating in a Likert scale rather than pairwise feedback, but they have a very similar structure.
if you look at the median wages, they're above $50 across a range of different topics. ... some of these experts are being paid more than $100 per hour to do annotation work.
getting verifiable annotators, especially ones where you're sure that they're not using AI. ... we have to check the correctness of these long chat responses in under a minute.
I think it's more of the latter. Maybe you need a lawyer to check if a Blue Book annotation is correct. ... they will use the cheapest LLM to generate plausible-looking answers.

provenance.filtering_note: p36 (the pairwise setup figure), p37 (InstructGPT labeling guideline), p38 (Bard annotation document, Bloomberg link), p39 (modern worker distribution) and p40 (compensation, Business Insider link) are screenshots; no pay figures, country shares or guideline text survive. The slide does not discuss alternatives to pairwise data (Likert ratings, rankings of k outputs as in InstructGPT, which the figure shows but the text does not). 'Have to be careful about AI use' is not explained: annotators using LMs to produce labels collapses the data toward the LM's preferences (ai-feedback-rlaif). p42's ethics claim is a headline over an image. Correction from the audio: the note said no pay figures, country shares or guideline text survive, and that alternatives to pairwise data are not discussed. Aloud: InstructGPT's guideline asks for helpful, truthful and harmless outputs, glossed as clear writing and not overly long answers, no hallucination, and up-weighting refusals of questionable prompts (47:50-48:18); the leaked Bard guideline rates on 'a Likert scale rather than pairwise feedback' with a similar structure (48:42-49:12), so one alternative is mentioned. The p39-p40 screenshots are read: on one Scale AI platform about 70% of annotators hold bachelor's or master's degrees and the modal age is about 35 (49:48-50:02); median wages are 'above $50' an hour and some experts get 'more than $100 per hour' (50:46-51:00). The p41 bullets are explained: annotators using ChatGPT is 'extremely, extremely difficult' to prevent (51:43-51:53), and Bard annotators said they had to check long responses 'in under a minute' (52:02-52:16). The note's reading of 'AI use' as collapsing labels toward the LM's preferences remains the author's. Spoken evidence (49:19-49:30, 52:22-52:57): the worker distribution has 'shifted upwards, more towards experts', but low-cost annotation has not gone away (a 'pyramid', a bifurcation like the wider economy; Scale AI's outsourcing 'got into quite a bit of trouble'). Spoken evidence (58:23-59:07, Q&A): experts are recruited mainly because only they can answer some questions (a lawyer to check a Blue Book citation), and also because unsupervised annotators 'will use the cheapest LLM to generate plausible-looking answers'.

knowledge_points.label: Who annotates shifts the model: demographics move behaviour and most annotators reward style over substance
knowledge_points.statement: The reward model encodes its annotators, so the annotator distribution for RLHF can significantly shift the model's behaviours and expressed opinions (Santurkar et al.), and annotators' preferences are dominated by style and assertiveness rather than factual accuracy for many annotators though not all (Hosking, Blunsom, Bartolo), which is why RLHF amplifies style.

anchors.quote: The annotator distribution for RLHF can significantly shift its behaviors
RLHF and style – annotators matter (a lot) ... This is true even for many annotators – but not all annotators

anchors.ref: santurkar2023:§5 (RLHF models' opinions shift toward specific demographic groups)
hosking2024:§4 (assertiveness and style drive preference; factuality under-weighted)

anchors.quote: annotators have a surprising amount of influence over what the model does. ... your annotation groups have biases, you can actually end up getting some pretty surprising behavior.

base models of various kinds were kind of similar to Protestants or Roman Catholic opinions ... more similar to Buddhist, Hindus, and atheists ... a lot of Southeast Asians, and also people in the West Coast of America.

non-expert annotators, that are just kind of paid on a platform really like to emphasize formatting effects ... things like factuality or inconsistency are things that are much more emphasized than the expert annotators.

provenance.filtering_note: Both slides are plots (image). Santurkar's finding that RLHF models' opinion distributions move toward liberal, educated, higher-income US respondents, and Hosking's that assertiveness predicts preference while factual errors are under-penalized, are from the papers; the slide text says only 'shift its behaviors' and 'annotators matter (a lot)'. 'Not all annotators' is the slide's hedge that some annotators do weigh factuality; no proportion is given. The slide does not say how to correct for annotator composition (reweighting, mixed panels). Spoken evidence (53:02-53:27): annotators have 'a surprising amount of influence' because post-training is the final shaping step before shipping. Spoken evidence (53:27-54:37), p43 read aloud: on opinion-poll questions base models sat close to Protestant and Roman Catholic respondents and far from Buddhist or Hindu ones; after post-training they moved toward Buddhists, Hindus and atheists, which the InstructGPT appendix explains: its annotators were largely Southeast Asian and US West Coast. (The note's 'liberal, educated, higher-income' summary is the paper's; the religion reading is what is said.) Spoken evidence (55:37-56:23), p44 read aloud: Hosking et al. compared expert annotators with platform crowdworkers; non-experts over-weight formatting, while factuality and inconsistency are weighted by the experts, and 'it's much, much harder to test for factuality'. The slide's 'not all annotators' therefore refers to the expert group. He adds that studies of LLM political opinions 'can be quite fragile and sketchy at times' (55:20). Spoken slip (54:51): the owl-preference transfer through innocuous model-generated data is called 'something called emergent misalignment'. That result is subliminal learning (Cloud et al. 2025); emergent misalignment (Betley et al. 2025) is broad misalignment after narrow fine-tuning on insecure code. He calls it 'subliminal transfer' a sentence later (55:07). Not imported; recorded as an aside in spoken_filtering.

misconceptions.belief: With enough annotators, individual biases average out and the reward model learns 'true' quality.
misconceptions.why_wrong: p44: the style-over-substance preference holds for many annotators, so it is a shared bias that averaging reinforces rather than cancels; p43: the panel's demographic distribution is itself a bias that averaging cannot remove.

misconceptions.belief: Annotator bias affects only subjective questions (opinions), not factual answers.
misconceptions.why_wrong: Hosking et al. (p44) is about factual outputs: annotators prefer assertive answers and under-penalize factual errors, so the reward model learns to reward confidence over correctness.

predict.q: Two RLHF runs differ only in the annotator pool: pool X is 500 US college students, pool Y is 500 annotators sampled to match a national survey. Per slide 43, what will differ between the resulting models?
predict.answer: Their behaviours and expressed opinions will shift toward their respective annotator pools; the pool-X model reflects college-student preferences and opinions, the pool-Y model a nationally representative mix.
predict.why: The reward model is fitted to the pool's judgements, and the policy optimizes that reward; the pool's distribution becomes the model's distribution.
predict.targets_misconception: With enough annotators, individual biases average out and the reward model learns 'true' quality.

transfer.q: A medical QA model after RLHF gives more confident, assertive answers but its factual error rate has not improved. Using p44, explain the mechanism and say what change to the annotation process (not the algorithm) would target it.
transfer.answer: Annotators rewarded assertiveness and under-penalized factual errors, so the reward model learned confidence as quality and the policy optimized it. Fix at the data level: have annotators (or expert annotators) verify facts, or make factuality an explicit, separately scored criterion.
transfer.why: Style bias in the labels is the root; no optimizer fixes a reward that does not measure correctness.
transfer.varies: functional: the observed symptom is confidence without accuracy in a factual domain rather than a shift in opinions
transfer.invariant: the reward model reproduces whatever its annotators actually reward

knowledge_points.label: Inter-annotator agreement measures variance, not bias
knowledge_points.statement: Inter-annotator agreement is a statement about the variance of a population of annotators, not their bias: high agreement can come from a shared bias, or from everyone pasting answers from the same chatbot (which drives the variance to zero), and low agreement can be inherent to subjective tasks; so agreement alone cannot certify annotation quality, and a detailed guideline with checkable criteria is the other route.

anchors.quote: The other notion of a good annotator is inter-annotator agreement. ... it doesn't tell you what the bias is. It tells you the variance. And some tasks inherently have variance. If you're asking do you like this, that's a task with lots of variance.
So inter-annotator agreement is not useful. ... Or if they're all using ChatGPT, the variance will also be zero. So it's very hard to assess quality
a sufficiently-detailed annotation guideline should hopefully be semi objective. ... Like in the first three pages of the Google search, you don't find anything that contradicts it.
Agreement near human inter-annotator levels

provenance.filtering_note: Spoken only (Q&A, 56:38-57:59). Asked what makes one annotator higher quality than another, the professor offers two notions. One is a sufficiently detailed guideline with objective criteria ('in the first three pages of the Google search, you don't find anything that contradicts it'), which lets you catch someone not following the rule. The other is inter-annotator agreement, 'a statement about a population of annotators', which 'doesn't tell you what the bias is. It tells you the variance'. It is uninformative for subjective tasks ('do you like this'), and its variance is zero if annotators 'are all using ChatGPT'. The captions are garbled around 57:43-57:51 ('If you're asking, is it factual, maybe it should be lower. But even if it's zero, if you've asked the right question.'); the KP uses only the clear sentences. The deck uses agreement as the yardstick for LM judges (p45: 'Agreement near human inter-annotator levels'), and this caveat qualifies it: matching the human agreement level says the judge's variance is human-like, not that it is unbiased (compare ai-feedback-rlaif's second misconception). The numbers in the prompts are the author's.

prerequisites.note: A Q&A right after the Hosking expert-vs-crowd result (56:38).

misconceptions.belief: High inter-annotator agreement shows that the labels are correct.
misconceptions.why_wrong: Agreement measures the variance across annotators, not their bias (57:32-57:36). A panel that shares a bias, or that copies every verdict from the same chatbot, agrees perfectly and can be consistently wrong.

misconceptions.belief: Low inter-annotator agreement means the annotators are careless.
misconceptions.why_wrong: Some tasks inherently have variance: disagreement on 'do you like this' reflects real differences in taste (57:37-57:43), so low agreement there is not evidence of bad annotators.

predict.q: A vendor delivers 10,000 preference labels with 97% inter-annotator agreement, far above the 70% your careful in-house annotators reached on a pilot batch. Logs show most pairs were judged within seconds. What explanation for the high agreement does the lecture raise, and what does agreement fail to tell you?
predict.answer: The annotators may all be using the same chatbot (e.g. ChatGPT), which drives the variance toward zero. Agreement measures variance, not bias, so it says nothing about whether the labels are right.
predict.why: 'If they're all using ChatGPT, the variance will also be zero' (57:51); agreement 'doesn't tell you what the bias is. It tells you the variance' (57:32).
predict.targets_misconception: High inter-annotator agreement shows that the labels are correct.

transfer.q: On the same responses you run two annotation tasks: (a) 'Which response do you like more?', with 58% agreement; (b) 'Does the response contain a factual error, by the guideline's rule that nothing in the first three search pages contradicts it?', with 91% agreement. A manager concludes that the task-(a) annotators are sloppy and that the task-(b) labels are reliable because they agree. What does the lecture say about each conclusion?
transfer.answer: (a) Low agreement is not evidence of sloppiness: liking is a task with inherent variance. (b) High agreement shows low variance, not absence of bias; what makes (b) checkable is the guideline's objective criterion, which lets you audit individual labels.
transfer.why: The professor separates the two notions of a good annotator: following a semi-objective guideline (auditable) and agreement (variance only), and notes that subjective tasks have variance by nature (57:01-57:43).
transfer.targets_misconception: Low inter-annotator agreement means the annotators are careless.
transfer.varies: two tasks of different subjectivity, instead of one vendor's suspicious batch
transfer.invariant: agreement is the variance of the annotator population and is silent on bias

near 100%, which shows the labels are reliable
near chance, since nobody actually read the pairs

check.invariant: agreement = low variance, not correctness
check.targets_misconception: High inter-annotator agreement shows that the labels are correct.

retrieval.answer: The variance of a population of annotators; it does not tell you their bias.

retrieval.answer: Following a sufficiently detailed, semi-objective guideline (with checkable criteria); and inter-annotator agreement, which only measures variance.
