knowledge_points.label: LM-generated preferences (GPT-4 judges, UltraFeedback, Constitutional AI) are the frontier's default RLHF data
knowledge_points.statement: GPT-4 is a surprisingly good pairwise feedback system: near-perfect rank correlation with humans at the system level and agreement near human inter-annotator levels, so for people following the frontier AI feedback is often used in place of human preferences (UltraFeedback in Zephyr, OLMo, Tulu 3), and Constitutional AI closes the loop with self-training where the model critiques and revises its own outputs.

anchors.quote: GPT4 is a surprisingly good pairwise feedback system ... Near-perfect rank correlation at the system level ... Agreement near human inter-annotator levels
For people following the frontier – AI feedback often used for RLHF ... Used in e.g. Olmo, Zephyr, etc
RLHF and data – Self-training ... From Constitutional AI, Bai et al.

anchors.ref: alpacafarm:§4 (simulated annotators agree with humans at ~65%)

anchors.quote: Model-based data annotation is quite good. ... Modern models are probably much, much better than random crowd worker you can get.
if you compare the rankings of systems, they're pretty good. ... And their cost is an order of magnitude less.
there's basically no space for human collected data if all you want to do is to catch up to the frontier and capabilities.

they found that it was extremely time-consuming, costly, and the results they were getting were not actually better than using model-based annotations. ... in the end, they ended up using AI feedback.
This was Constitutional AI, where they kind of prompted a model to generate safety data, and then they trained the model itself on that prompted data.
But if you want something like lawyers or scientists, you can't get world knowledge without getting people to annotate.

provenance.filtering_note: p45's two plots (system-level rank correlation; per-pair agreement) are images and the slide text gives no correlation coefficient or agreement percentage; the AlpacaFarm value (~65% agreement, matching human-human agreement) is from the paper. p46 shows the UltraFeedback, Zephyr 7b and Tulu 3 figures as images with a substack link. p47 is the Constitutional AI figure only; the slide does not describe the critique-revision loop or the 'constitution'. The slide does not say what AI feedback inherits: the length bias of p17 (the judge is the same kind of model) and the self-preference of a model judging its own family. Correction from the audio: the note said the slide does not say what AI feedback inherits. Aloud: models 'are also very susceptible to the same kinds of biases as humans, sometimes in ways that are quite problematic as well, even more problematic', followed by the length results (1:04:30-1:05:23, recorded on length-bias-preferences). Spoken evidence (1:00:14-1:00:44): the p45 comparison was the professor's group's; GPT-4's system rankings and its agreement with the human majority are 'pretty good', at a cost 'an order of magnitude less'. Still no coefficient. Spoken evidence (1:00:46-1:02:46): 'there's basically no space for human collected data if all you want to do is to catch up to the frontier'; Hugging Face's Zephyr tried human data from the same vendors as the big labs and found it costly and 'not actually better', so it used AI feedback (the Q&A at 1:03:02 confirms this was at 7B scale); UltraChat and UltraFeedback are now standard, and Tulu 3 'uses model-based annotations for all of its pipeline'. Pushing the frontier still needs human data (1:02:49-1:02:55), as does world knowledge from lawyers or scientists (1:04:18-1:04:25). Spoken evidence (59:20-1:00:02, Q&A): domain-specific models have no unique advantage as annotators, because they are rarely better than the strongest open models. Spoken evidence (1:03:40-1:04:14): Constitutional AI is described in one sentence (prompted to generate safety data, then trained on it) as 'a very early self post-training data generation loop', with Self-Instruct as the capability-centric analogue; the critique-revision steps and the constitution are still not described.

prerequisites.note: The GPT-based judge of p17 is the same instrument p45 praises; its length effect carries into the AI-feedback data.

misconceptions.why_wrong: p45: GPT-4's agreement with humans is near the human inter-annotator level, so on the metric that matters (agreement with a held-out human) it is about as good as another human; this is why the frontier uses it.

misconceptions.belief: Because GPT-4 agrees with humans, its labels are free of the human biases of p43-p44 and p17.
misconceptions.why_wrong: Agreement with humans means it reproduces human judgements, biases included: p17 shows the same strong length effect in GPT-based evaluation, and p46-p47 self-training loops add self-preference.

predict.q: You replace your human annotators with GPT-4 for pairwise labels. Per slide 45, roughly where does GPT-4's agreement with a human label land relative to agreement between two humans, and what does that imply about the ceiling of any single annotator?
predict.answer: Near the human inter-annotator level: GPT-4 agrees with a human about as often as another human would. The ceiling is the inter-annotator agreement itself; no annotator, human or LM, can exceed it on noisy preferences.
predict.why: Per-pair agreement is bounded by how consistent the humans are with each other; matching that bound is the best any judge can show on this metric.
predict.targets_misconception: AI feedback is a cheap approximation that is clearly worse than human labels.

transfer.q: A team generates all RLHF preference labels with their own model judging its own outputs (as in a Constitutional-AI-style self-training loop, p47). Name two biases from earlier in the lecture that this setup inherits or worsens, and one property from p45 that still makes it attractive.
transfer.answer: Inherits the length/style bias of LM judges (p17) and the annotator-distribution bias of whatever trained the judge (p43-p44), plus self-preference for its own style. Still attractive because LM judges reach near-human agreement at scale and near-perfect system-level ranking (p45), at near-zero marginal cost.
transfer.why: An LM judge is a learned reward model trained on human preferences; it reproduces their biases, and judging oneself adds correlation between policy and judge.
transfer.varies: functional: the judge is the policy's own model rather than an external GPT-4
transfer.invariant: an LM judge agrees with humans by reproducing their preferences, biases included

knowledge_points.label: Reward model: Bradley-Terry fit to pairs, P(chosen) = sigmoid(r_w - r_l), so only reward differences are identified
knowledge_points.statement: The Stiennon-style reward model turns pairwise feedback into a scalar reward by assuming a Bradley-Terry model, P(y_w preferred over y_l | x) = sigmoid(r(x,y_w) - r(x,y_l)), and maximizing the log-likelihood of the observed choices; the assumptions are that preferences are transitive and depend only on a reward difference, so the reward is identified only up to an additive per-prompt constant, and already well-separated pairs contribute vanishing gradient.

anchors.quote: We can now optimize the implied reward as a reward model via the Stiennon objective
More details and background from Stiennon ... From "Learning to summarize from human feedback"
Standard 'pairwise feedback' setup
Train a reward model, get 1024 LM outputs, take the best one.

The model is going to generate a couple of different outputs. ... A rater comes in and rates all of the examples and provides a ranking over the examples. ... we go through the reward model because it might be easier to train a verifier than to train a model that does well directly.
the reward in this case is a pairwise feedback model that you've learned. So you train a binary classifier on which of a pair of examples is better. And then you hill climb on that reward.

provenance.filtering_note: The reward-model loss is never written in the text layer: p52 shows it as a screenshot from Stiennon et al. and p57 refers to it as 'the Stiennon objective' inside the DPO derivation. The name Bradley-Terry does not appear on any slide (the DPO paper uses it); the formula, the transitivity assumption and the shift-invariance are from the papers in sources.json and are the author's framing of what 'the Stiennon objective' is. The slide does not mention reward-model initialization from the SFT model, per-prompt normalization, or that InstructGPT ranks K outputs and expands them into pairs. Spoken evidence (1:06:39-1:06:55): the Stiennon reward model is described aloud as 'a binary classifier on which of a pair of examples is better', then hill-climbed. The name Bradley-Terry and the sigmoid-of-difference formula are still not said, so the framing remains the author's from the papers. Spoken evidence (46:23-47:07), the pipeline overview: candidates are sampled 'with temperature one' because the SFT model 'is pretty diverse'; a rater ranks them ('sometimes, even a binary ranking'), so ranking more than two outputs is mentioned, which partly answers the note's 'InstructGPT ranks K outputs'; the reason to go through a reward model is that 'it might be easier to train a verifier than to train a model that does well directly'.

prerequisites.note: The pairs are the reward model's training data.
The reward model is how 'a reward we can measure' is manufactured from judgements.

misconceptions.belief: The reward model learns an absolute quality score; a reward of 2.0 means the same thing for every prompt.
misconceptions.why_wrong: The Bradley-Terry likelihood depends only on r_w - r_l, so adding any constant per prompt leaves the loss unchanged; rewards are comparable only within a prompt unless an extra normalization is imposed.

misconceptions.belief: A reward model trained on pairs returns the probability that a response is good.
misconceptions.why_wrong: It returns an unnormalized scalar; sigmoid of a difference of two such scalars is the probability that one response beats another. A single response has no probability of being good under this model.

predict.q: A reward model scores the chosen response 3.0 and the rejected one 1.0. Under the Bradley-Terry model of the Stiennon objective, what probability does it assign to the annotator's choice, and how does that probability change if both scores are raised by 10?
predict.answer: sigmoid(3.0 - 1.0) = sigmoid(2) ≈ 0.88; raising both by 10 leaves it at 0.88, since only the difference enters.
predict.why: P(y_w > y_l) = sigmoid(r_w - r_l); any common shift cancels inside the difference, which is why absolute reward values are not identified by pairs.
predict.targets_misconception: The reward model learns an absolute quality score; a reward of 2.0 means the same thing for every prompt.

transfer.q: You fit the same Bradley-Terry model to chess results instead of text pairs: player ratings r_i, P(i beats j) = sigmoid(r_i - r_j). An annotator-like data set says A beats B 90% of the time, B beats C 90% of the time, and C beats A 90% of the time. Explain which Bradley-Terry assumption this violates and what the fitted model will do with it.
transfer.answer: It violates transitivity (a single scalar per item implies A > B > C implies A > C). No ratings fit all three; the maximum-likelihood fit compromises, pulling the three ratings toward each other and assigning roughly 50% to each pair, so the cyclic preferences are averaged away.
transfer.why: Bradley-Terry represents every item by one number; cyclic or context-dependent preferences cannot be represented and show up as low-margin, under-confident fits.
transfer.varies: domain: chess players instead of responses; the changed feature is a cyclic (intransitive) preference pattern
transfer.invariant: one scalar per item and a sigmoid of differences, hence transitivity is forced

check.q: A Bradley-Terry reward model, P(a preferred over b) = sigmoid(r(a) - r(b)), assigns P(A over B) = 0.8 and P(B over C) = 0.8 for one prompt. What probability does it then imply for A preferred over C? Give a decimal.
check.why: sigmoid(d) = 0.8 means d = ln(0.8/0.2) = ln 4. A single scalar reward per response makes differences add: r(A) - r(C) = 2 ln 4 = ln 16, so P(A over C) = 16/17 ≈ 0.941. This additivity is the transitivity a cyclic data set cannot satisfy.
check.varies: consistent preferences and a numeric consequence, instead of cyclic preferences the model cannot fit
check.invariant: Bradley-Terry gives each response one scalar reward, so reward differences add and preferences are transitive
check.targets_misconception: The reward model learns an absolute quality score; a reward of 2.0 means the same thing for every prompt.

retrieval.q: Write the Bradley-Terry probability that the chosen response beats the rejected one in terms of the reward model r.
retrieval.answer: sigmoid(r(x, y_w) - r(x, y_l)).

retrieval.q: Which quantity is left unidentified when a reward model is trained only on pairwise comparisons?
retrieval.answer: The absolute level (an additive constant per prompt); only reward differences are determined.

retrieval.q: DPO reuses the pairwise reward-model loss of an earlier RLHF paper. Whose objective does the lecture name it after?
retrieval.answer: Stiennon's: 'the Stiennon objective', from 'Learning to summarize from human feedback' (the Bradley-Terry pairwise loss).

steps.why: Bradley-Terry turns two scalar rewards into a choice probability that depends only on their difference, so a binary classifier on pairs can train a scalar reward.

The Stiennon objective is the negative log-likelihood of the observed choices. Its gradient is the remaining error 1 − P, so pairs that are already well separated barely teach anything.

steps.why: Only differences enter. Pairs therefore fix the reward only up to a constant per prompt.

knowledge_points.label: PPO for RLHF: policy gradient is too high-variance, TRPO linearizes, PPO clips ratios; the InstructGPT objective looks innocuous
knowledge_points.statement: InstructGPT optimizes the reward-model score with PPO under an objective that looks innocuous; conceptually the ideas are: policy gradients estimate grad E[R(z)] as E[R(z) grad log p(z)] but the variance is too high, TRPO linearizes the problem around the current policy, and PPO clips the probability ratios at some eps; the professor calls PPO 'the original and very finicky approach' and gives only the brief version here.

anchors.quote: Attempt 1: Policy gradients (variances are too high) ... Attempt 2: TRPO (Linearize the problem around the current policy) ... Attempt 3: PPO (Clip the ratios at some eps)
PPO in language modeling From InstructGPT ... ..this is very innocuous looking
Part 1: PPO – the original and very finicky approach (the brief version)

anchors.ref: instructgpt:eq. 2 (RM reward - beta KL to SFT + gamma pretraining LM term)

anchors.quote: I'm going to maximize, under my policy, the reward that I get by sampling from that policy. ... this is like baby reinforcement learning. ... people might say we're playing bandits.

it appears almost exactly in the InstructGPT paper. ... subject to this second term, which is really just a KL divergence. ... I want to stay close to my pre-trained model because I don't want to go too far and become degenerate.

the very basic starting point is the policy gradient identity. ... I'm just going to take the gradient of my log probabilities and weigh it by my rewards. And this really just looks like SFT, but with weighted examples, effectively.

the problem with policy gradients is I need to sample every time I want to take an optimization step. ... I want to roll out once, and I want to reuse that rollout multiple times. ... So this is something called TRPO.
PPO says, well, TRPO is a good idea, but this distance constraint is actually kind of hard to deal with. ... I'm going to come up with a heuristic clipping thing

provenance.filtering_note: The InstructGPT objective on p51 is an image: its reward-model term, the per-token KL penalty beta * log(pi_RL / pi_SFT) to the SFT model and the pretraining-mix term gamma * E[log pi_RL(x)] on pretraining data are named here from the paper, not the text layer; the slide calls the whole thing 'very innocuous looking' to foreshadow p61-p63. The policy-gradient identity on p53 is in the text layer but with garbled math glyphs, so it is paraphrased. The slide does not derive the log-derivative trick, define TRPO's constraint, or say why variance is high; lecture 16 (policy-gradient-variance, ppo-ratio-clip, per-token-kl-reward-shaping) expands all three and is the thread to send a learner to. Correction from the audio: the note said the KL penalty is named 'from the paper, not the text layer'. It is said aloud (1:06:10-1:06:39): InstructGPT's equation 2 maximizes reward 'subject to this second term, which is really just a KL divergence', to stay close and not 'become degenerate'. The pretraining-mix term is not said. Spoken slip (1:06:31): he says the KL keeps the policy close to 'my pre-trained model'; InstructGPT's KL is to the SFT model (as in the statement and the first misconception), and pretraining data enters through the separate gamma term. Not imported. Spoken evidence (1:07:46-1:08:31): the reason given aloud for moving past plain policy gradients is not the slide's variance: sampling every step is expensive (inference is hard, training is arithmetically intense), so you want to 'roll out once' and reuse it, which is off-policy; TRPO takes several steps while staying close, with 'an importance weighting correction' ('I'm not going to go into that in detail'), and PPO replaces the hard distance constraint with 'a heuristic clipping thing'. Variance is never mentioned aloud. The statement and the second misconception keep p53's variance framing (no explicit correction); lecture_16:ppo-ratio-clip covers rollout reuse. Spoken evidence (1:05:53-1:06:07, 1:07:36-1:07:46): RLHF is 'baby reinforcement learning', a bandit rather than multi-turn RL (lecture_16:language-rl-is-a-bandit), and the policy gradient 'really just looks like SFT, but with weighted examples'. prerequisites.note: PPO maximizes the reward model's score.

The KL-to-SFT term of the InstructGPT objective (image on p51) is implemented as per-token reward shaping in lecture 16 p14.

misconceptions.belief: The RLHF objective is just 'maximize the reward model score'.
misconceptions.why_wrong: The InstructGPT objective (p51 image, paper eq. 2) also penalizes KL from the SFT model and mixes in a pretraining loss; without them the policy drifts to reward-hacking outputs (p62-p63) and forgets pretraining. 'Innocuous looking' is the professor's warning that the simple form hides this.

misconceptions.belief: PPO is a different objective from the policy gradient.
misconceptions.why_wrong: p53 frames TRPO and PPO as two fixes for the variance of the same objective, grad E[R]; PPO's clipping bounds how far one batch can move the ratio, it does not change what is being maximized.

predict.q: An engineer implements RLHF as 'sample from the policy, score with the reward model, take a plain policy-gradient step'. Per slide 53, what is the first thing the professor expects to go wrong?
choices: The gradient is biased because the reward is not differentiable
The gradient estimate's variance is too high for stable training
The policy cannot move because the reward model is frozen
predict.answer: The gradient estimate's variance is too high for stable training
predict.why: 'Attempt 1: Policy gradients (variances are too high)' is the diagnosis; TRPO and PPO exist to make the step size safe, not to fix bias or differentiability.
predict.targets_misconception: PPO is a different objective from the policy gradient.
predict.distractor_from: option 1: the belief that non-differentiable rewards bias the estimator (they do not; R only weights grad log p); option 3: confusing a frozen reward model with a frozen policy

transfer.q: In an RLHF run with the KL-to-SFT term removed from the InstructGPT objective, reward-model score climbs steadily for 2,000 steps. Using p51's 'innocuous looking' warning and p62, say what you expect the human-judged quality to do over those steps and which term was holding it in check.
transfer.answer: Human-judged quality rises then falls while the reward score keeps climbing (overoptimization of the proxy); the KL penalty to the SFT model was the term keeping the policy near a distribution where the reward model is trustworthy.
transfer.why: The reward model is accurate only near the data it was trained on; the KL term bounds drift from that region, and removing it lets PPO exploit the model.
transfer.varies: functional: the KL term is ablated rather than present; the question is about the consequence for the objective's hidden safeguards
transfer.invariant: PPO maximizes the reward model score; whatever bounds the policy's drift is what prevents exploitation

check.q: In an InstructGPT-style objective (reward-model score minus beta times the KL divergence from the SFT model), beta is raised tenfold and everything else is kept. Which way does the policy's KL divergence from the SFT model at the end of training move? Start with up, down or same.
check.answer: Down: a larger KL penalty holds the policy closer to the SFT model, trading some reward-model score for staying where the reward model is trustworthy.
check.why: p51: the objective is not just 'maximize the reward model'; it includes a KL term to the SFT policy. Raising its weight makes drifting from SFT more costly, so the optimum sits at a smaller KL.
check.varies: the KL weight is increased rather than removed
check.invariant: the KL-to-SFT term restrains the policy's drift while it maximizes the proxy reward
check.targets_misconception: The RLHF objective is just 'maximize the reward model score'.

retrieval.q: In the lecture's three attempts (policy gradients, then a middle step, then PPO), which method is the middle step and what does it do?
retrieval.answer: TRPO: it linearizes the problem around the current policy (plain policy gradients have too much variance; PPO then clips the ratios at some eps).

retrieval.q: What adjective does the lecture use for the InstructGPT PPO objective, a description its later warnings about overoptimization and mode collapse undercut?
retrieval.answer: 'Very innocuous looking'.

retrieval.q: How does the lecture characterize PPO relative to DPO?
retrieval.answer: PPO: the original and very finicky approach; DPO: the new, very accessible approach.

prompts.self_explain: Why does a method that only clips how far probabilities move per step count as the fix for a variance problem?

steps.do: Attempt 1, policy gradients: sample from the policy, weight each sample's log-likelihood gradient by its reward.
steps.why: The reward model's score is only a scalar on sampled text, so the gradient has to go through log p. That makes it 'SFT, but with weighted examples' (1:07:14). The sample estimate's variance is too high, and every step needs fresh samples.

steps.do: Attempt 2, TRPO: roll out once, reuse the rollout for several steps, and linearize the problem around the current policy while staying close to it.
steps.why: Reusing rollouts is only safe while the new policy stays near the one that produced them. TRPO enforces that with a distance constraint, and the constraint is hard to handle (1:08:33).

steps.do: Attempt 3, PPO: replace the constraint with a heuristic, clipping the probability ratio π_new/π_old at 1 ± ε.
steps.why: Clipping removes the incentive to move a token's ratio outside the band. It keeps most of TRPO's safety and none of its constrained optimization. Lecture 16 (ppo-ratio-clip) works the clip itself.

presentations.notice: Raising β pulls the filled bars back onto the π_ref outlines and the KL readout falls; along the curve the proxy reward only rises with KL, while the gold reward peaks and then falls, which is the region the KL term keeps the policy out of.
listen for: policy gradient as 'SFT, but with weighted examples', then 'roll out once ... reuse that rollout', TRPO's closeness and PPO's 'heuristic clipping'

knowledge_points.label: Avoiding on-policy RL: control tokens, SFT on preferred, RM-filtered SFT, best-of-1024
knowledge_points.statement: Because on-policy RL (PPO) is finicky, people tried to use pairwise data without it: SFT on both outputs with a control token ([GOOD] prepended to chosen, [BAD] to rejected); SFT on only the preferred outputs; train a reward model, sample LM outputs and SFT on the ones it prefers; or train a reward model, sample 1024 outputs and return the best (best-of-n at inference); all are reasonable, and DPO is the one that keeps the optimization view without rollouts.

anchors.quote: Question for many: can we avoid doing any 'RL' ? (i.e. on-policy RL algorithms)
Train the model with a control token – (SFT on the pairs, prepend [GOOD] to chosen, [BAD] to not chosen) ... Train the model on only preferred output
Train a reward model, get LM outputs, train on the preferred output ... Train a reward model, get 1024 LM outputs, take the best one.
DPO + Expert iteration for post-training
PPO, already, the equations look a little bit gnarly. ... Can we get rid of PPO? ... I will tell them to you so that you do not necessarily repeat them in your own research.
For the pair that's good, I will prepend a good token. ... So this is reducing PPO to SFT or RL to SFT. It does not work.
People have tried training the model only on the good stuff. Also does not work very well. ... That does not work as well, although it does somewhat work.

provenance.filtering_note: p54 lists the four alternatives without naming them (conditional training / Quark / SteerLM for control tokens; RAFT / rejection-sampling fine-tuning for RM-filtered SFT; best-of-n sampling) and without results; the professor says only 'some reasonable stuff people thought about'. The deck does not say which failed or why (the first two never use the rejected output as a negative signal; best-of-n is an inference-time method that costs 1024x compute per query). p59's 'DPO + Expert iteration' (Llama 3 rounds of rejection sampling SFT then DPO) shows that the third alternative became a standard component alongside DPO. The number 1024 is in the text layer. Correction from the audio: the note said 'the professor says only 'some reasonable stuff people thought about'. The deck does not say which failed'. Aloud he grades them, offered 'so that you do not necessarily repeat them in your own research' (1:09:18): the control-token variant 'does not work'; training only on the preferred outputs 'also does not work very well'; reward-model-filtered SFT 'does not work as well, although it does somewhat work' (1:09:23-1:10:03). Best-of-1024 is not mentioned aloud. The statement keeps the slide's 'all are reasonable' (reasonable ideas, which he does not retract); the outcomes are recorded here. His 'somewhat work' for the third option sits beside his own account of Llama's outer loop (1:14:46-1:15:04), where DPO is combined with rejection sampling, which is that option used as a component.

prerequisites.note: Two of the four alternatives start with 'train a reward model'.

misconceptions.belief: SFT on only the preferred outputs uses all the information in a pairwise dataset.
misconceptions.why_wrong: It discards the rejected output entirely; the pair's information is the contrast. The control-token variant and DPO (p55 'negative gradient steps on bad stuff') are the alternatives that use the rejected side.

misconceptions.belief: Best-of-n with a reward model changes the model's weights.
misconceptions.why_wrong: p54's fourth option samples 1024 outputs and takes the best at inference; the policy is untouched and every query pays the 1024x sampling cost, unless the selected outputs are then used for SFT (the third option).

predict.q: You have 50k (prompt, chosen, rejected) triples and no RL infrastructure. Of the p54 options 'SFT on only preferred outputs' and 'control token SFT on both', which one lets the model learn anything from the rejected responses, and how is that information encoded?
predict.answer: Control-token SFT: the rejected response is trained on too, but with [BAD] prepended, so the model learns to associate the two styles with the tokens and is then prompted with [GOOD]. SFT on preferred only never sees the rejected text.
predict.why: Pairwise data's signal is the contrast between the two; only methods that condition on or penalize the rejected side keep it.
predict.targets_misconception: SFT on only the preferred outputs uses all the information in a pairwise dataset.

transfer.q: A product team serves a model by sampling 64 candidates per request and returning the one a reward model prefers. Place this on p54's list, state what it shares with 'train a reward model, get LM outputs, train on the preferred output', and name the cost that distinguishes them at serving time.
transfer.answer: It is the best-of-n option (p54's '1024 outputs, take the best one' with n = 64). Both rank samples with a reward model; the difference is that best-of-n pays 64x generation cost on every request while RM-filtered SFT amortizes the selection into the weights once.
transfer.why: Both alternatives turn a reward model into a selection signal; one applies it at inference, the other at training.
transfer.varies: the value of n (64 instead of 1024) and the stage where selection is applied
transfer.invariant: a reward model ranks samples from the policy; the two options differ only in whether the ranking is distilled into weights

check.q: A team serves a model with best-of-1024 sampling against a reward model for a month, then switches back to returning a single sample per request. Compared with the single samples from before the best-of-n month, which way does single-sample quality move? Start with up, down or same.
check.answer: Same: best-of-n only selects among samples at inference; it never updates the weights, so single samples are as good as before.
check.why: p54: 'train a reward model, get 1024 LM outputs, take the best one' is selection at serving time. Unlike RM-filtered SFT, which trains on the preferred outputs, it leaves the model's weights unchanged.
check.varies: asks what persists after best-of-n stops, instead of placing a best-of-64 server on the list
check.invariant: best-of-n selects at inference; only the training-based options change the weights
check.targets_misconception: Best-of-n with a reward model changes the model's weights.

retrieval.q: Of the lecture's four ways to use pairwise feedback without on-policy RL, which one trains on both the chosen and the rejected output, and how?
retrieval.answer: SFT on both outputs with a control token: [GOOD] prepended to the chosen one, [BAD] to the rejected one.

retrieval.q: How many LM outputs does the lecture's best-of-n option sample?
What does 'RL' mean in the lecture's question 'can we avoid doing any RL?'
retrieval.answer: On-policy RL algorithms (rollouts from the current policy, e.g. PPO).

knowledge_points.label: DPO: nonparametric optimum gives r = beta log(pi/pi_ref) + const; plug into Bradley-Terry; MLE on pairs
knowledge_points.statement: DPO removes the reward model and all on-policy machinery by (1) assuming the policy class is all policies, so the KL-regularized RLHF objective's maximizer is pi*(y|x) ∝ pi_ref(y|x) exp(r(x,y)/beta), (2) solving for the implied reward r = beta log(pi/pi_ref) + beta log Z(x) and parametrizing the reward through the policy, and (3) optimizing that reward with the Stiennon (Bradley-Terry) loss on pairs, where the partition function cancels in the difference; the resulting gradient is a positive step on the chosen response and a negative step on the rejected one, scaled by the implied reward model's prediction error, and DPO equals RLHF's optimum only under the nonparametric assumption and the same pairwise data distribution.

anchors.quote: Getting rid of the reward model ... Getting rid of any on-policy stuff (rollouts, outer loops etc) ... Take gradient steps on log-loss of good stuff ... Take negative gradient steps on bad stuff (appropriately weighted).
is the set of all policies (nonparametric assumption). The maximizer is then, ... Solve for the 'implied reward' ... (This is the equivalence also used in the kimi-think paper)

2. Parametrize reward r via the policy ... 3. Optimize the reward using supervised losses (which in turn, optimizes the policy) ... This is MLE on the pairwise rewards, under nonparametric assumption + alternative parametrization
In some sense, reduces to "pos gradient on good, neg gradient on bad" ... (Scaled by 'prediction error' of the implied reward model)
But PPO does too (and sometimes better?) ... Lots of results are highly contingent (on the specifics of the experiment setup)

anchors.ref: dpo:§4 eq. 4-7 (optimal policy, implicit reward, DPO loss, gradient)
kimi:§2.3 (closed-form optimal policy reused for the squared-loss objective)

anchors.quote: We're going to get rid of the reward model. We're going to get rid of anything that has to do with on-policy stuff.

we're going to take steps in the direction of the log loss of the good stuff. ... we will take negative gradient steps on the direction of the bad stuff. ... if you wait these two appropriately, you will get an algorithm that is actually pretty good.

I'm going to assume that pi, my policy, is actually not a neural network at all. It is the set of all possible policies. ... take my original reference policy, and to exponentially tilt it by my reward.
I can solve for the implied reward. ... I plug-in my reward into that objective here, into my loss. And this gives the DPO objective

I'm going to increase the likelihood of the example, that one, and I'm going to decrease the likelihood of the example that lost. ... I'm going to scale the step size in some sense by how much my implied reward model is wrong.
maybe it doesn't matter very much, unless you're like at the frontier training the very best model. ... the core RLHF primitive for Llama was DPO.
these results are very, very contingent on the specifics of the experiment setup. ... if you do DPO right, you can do better than PPO.

prerequisites.note: Step 3 plugs the implied reward into the Stiennon objective.
DPO is the answer to p54's 'can we avoid doing any RL'.
The KL-regularized objective DPO solves is the InstructGPT PPO objective.

misconceptions.belief: DPO has no reward model, so it has no notion of reward.
misconceptions.why_wrong: p56-p57: DPO parametrizes the reward through the policy, r = beta log(pi/pi_ref) + const; the policy is the reward model ('your language model is secretly a reward model'), and the loss is the same Bradley-Terry MLE as reward-model training.

misconceptions.belief: DPO is exactly equivalent to PPO-RLHF, so the choice is only about engineering convenience.
misconceptions.why_wrong: The equivalence (p56) needs the nonparametric assumption (all policies) and holds at the optimum for the preference data's distribution; with a finite network and off-policy data they differ, which is why p61 reports PPO sometimes doing better and results being highly contingent.

misconceptions.belief: DPO's gradient is a constant positive push on chosen and negative push on rejected, like control-token SFT.
misconceptions.why_wrong: p58: the push is scaled by the prediction error of the implied reward model, sigmoid(r_hat_l - r_hat_w); pairs the implicit reward already orders correctly with a large margin get almost no gradient.

predict.q: At the start of DPO training the policy equals the reference model. For any pair, what is the implied reward of each response and what is the weight on the gradient (as a fraction of beta)?
predict.answer: Both implied rewards are beta log(pi/pi_ref) = 0, so the margin is 0, the implied preference probability is 0.5, and the gradient weight is beta * (1 - 0.5) = beta/2 for every pair regardless of how (un)likely the responses are.
predict.why: The implied reward measures deviation from the reference, not absolute likelihood; with no deviation yet, every pair is maximally uncertain under the implied reward model and receives the same weight.
predict.targets_misconception: DPO has no reward model, so it has no notion of reward.

transfer.q: Two DPO runs on the same data: run A raises log pi(y_w) by 5 nats and leaves y_l alone; run B leaves y_w alone and lowers log pi(y_l) by 5 nats. Compare the two runs' loss on that pair and say what this implies about what DPO is guaranteed to increase.
transfer.answer: Identical loss: the DPO margin depends only on the difference beta[(log pi(y_w) - log pi_ref(y_w)) - (log pi(y_l) - log pi_ref(y_l))], so +5 on the chosen and -5 on the rejected give the same margin. DPO is guaranteed to increase the margin, not the probability of the chosen response; the chosen response's likelihood can even fall.
transfer.why: Parametrizing the reward through log-ratios and feeding a Bradley-Terry loss makes the objective a function of the difference alone; which side moves is not constrained.
transfer.varies: functional: which response's log-probability moves (chosen up vs rejected down)
transfer.invariant: the DPO loss is a function of the implied-reward margin only

check.q: In DPO with beta = 0.1, after some training log pi(y_w) - log pi_ref(y_w) = -1.0 for the chosen response and log pi(y_l) - log pi_ref(y_l) = -4.0 for the rejected one. What preference probability, sigmoid(margin), does the implied reward model now assign to y_w over y_l? Give a decimal.
check.why: Implied rewards are beta log(pi/pi_ref): -0.1 for y_w and -0.4 for y_l (log Z cancels). Margin = 0.3, so sigmoid(0.3) ≈ 0.574 > 0.5, even though the chosen response became less likely than under the reference.
check.varies: both log-ratios move down by different amounts, and the item asks for the implied preference probability
check.invariant: DPO's loss depends only on the margin of implied rewards beta log(pi/pi_ref), not on the chosen likelihood itself
check.targets_misconception: DPO has no reward model, so it has no notion of reward.

retrieval.q: State the three key steps of the DPO derivation.
retrieval.answer: Make a nonparametric assumption linking policy and reward in closed form; parametrize the reward via the policy; optimize the reward with supervised (pairwise) losses, which optimizes the policy.

retrieval.q: Write DPO's implied reward in terms of the policy, the reference policy and beta.
retrieval.answer: r(x, y) = beta log(pi(y|x) / pi_ref(y|x)) + beta log Z(x); the Z term cancels in pairwise differences.

retrieval.q: What scales the positive-on-good, negative-on-bad gradient in DPO?
retrieval.answer: The prediction error of the implied reward model (how wrong the implicit preference probability currently is).

retrieval.q: What two things does DPO get rid of relative to PPO?
retrieval.answer: The reward model, and any on-policy machinery (rollouts, outer loops).

retrieval.q: What is the lecture's caution about PPO-vs-DPO comparisons?
retrieval.answer: PPO sometimes does as well or better; results are highly contingent on the experimental setup.

presentations.notice: The loss depends only on Δ_w − Δ_l: the 'chosen +5 only' and 'rejected −5 only' presets sit on the same diagonal with the same loss; at 'start' both implied rewards are 0 and the weight is exactly β/2; 'both lowered' has a loss below 0.693 while its point lies in the region where the chosen response is less likely than under π_ref.

steps.why: This is the KL-regularized RLHF objective (p51, p56). The nonparametric assumption lets π be any distribution, so it can be solved per prompt in closed form.
The objective equals −β·KL(π ‖ π*) + β log Z(x), so it is maximized exactly at π = π*. That is the reference policy exponentially tilted by the reward (1:11:34).
Take logs and solve for r. Any policy now defines an 'implied reward', so a reward can be parametrized through the policy.

steps.tex: P(y_w\succ y_l\mid x) = \sigma\!\Big(\beta\log\frac{\pi_\theta(y_w\mid x)}{\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}(y_w\mid x)} - \beta\log\frac{\pi_\theta(y_l\mid x)}{\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}(y_l\mid x)}\Big)
steps.why: Substitute into Bradley-Terry. Z(x) depends only on the prompt, so β log Z(x) is the same for both responses and cancels. That removes the intractable sum over all y.
This is the Stiennon pairwise MLE with the implied reward plugged in. It is a supervised loss on a fixed dataset, with no reward model and no rollouts (p55, p57).

The professor (1:17:12-1:17:27) calls the KL regularizer critical 'at least if your optimization process is very good': regularization limits how far an imperfect reward is exploited, but with a perfect reward there is nothing to exploit.

transfer.q: Slide 63's right panel shows no overoptimization when preferences come from a noiseless LM judge. A team therefore proposes to label with GPT-4 and 'optimize as hard as we like'. Using the p45 agreement result and the left/middle panels, explain why this does not deliver the right panel's immunity in practice.
transfer.answer: The right panel is immune because the reward model can match a deterministic judge exactly, so the proxy equals the target. GPT-4 labels in practice are noisy relative to the thing you care about (human preference; p45 says agreement is only at human inter-annotator level), so the trained reward is the middle panel's noisy-LM case, which does overoptimize.
transfer.why: Overoptimization is driven by the gap between proxy and target; a noiseless judge closes it only if that judge is the target you actually want.
transfer.varies: functional: the source of preference labels (deterministic LM vs GPT-4 as a stand-in for humans)
transfer.invariant: overoptimization exists iff the proxy reward and the true target disagree somewhere the policy can reach

check.q: A best-of-n system with no gradient training picks the output a reward model trained on human preferences scores highest. Compared with a moderate n, which way does true human preference for the selected output move at a very large n? Start with up, down or same.

check.why: p63: across many RLHF-style optimizers, best-of-n included, optimizing for the learned reward overfits past a point when the reward is fit to human preferences. The mechanism is the proxy's error, not PPO or gradient training.
check.varies: the optimizer is best-of-n selection rather than training on GPT-4 labels
check.invariant: optimizing a learned, noisy reward hard enough decouples it from the true preference
check.targets_misconception: Overoptimization is a PPO instability; DPO, which has no reward model, is immune.

knowledge_points.statement: Because RLHF maximizes a reward rather than fitting a distribution, the trained model is no longer a probabilistic model of text: it collapses toward high-reward modes (entropy drops) and its token probabilities are no longer calibrated to correctness by default, so confidence has to be re-estimated separately if it is needed.

misconceptions.belief: An RLHF model's token probability for an answer is its confidence that the answer is correct.
misconceptions.why_wrong: p64: RLHF models are no longer probabilistic models and have no calibration by default; the probability reflects what the reward favoured, which pushes mass onto preferred modes regardless of correctness.

misconceptions.belief: Mode collapse means the model produces nonsense.
misconceptions.why_wrong: p62's mode collapse is loss of entropy: outputs become fewer and more similar (the high-reward modes), typically fluent and confident; the cost is diversity and calibration, not coherence.

predict.q: A base model answers multiple-choice questions with probabilities that track its accuracy (70% probability means roughly 70% correct). After RLHF, per slide 64, what happens to that relationship and in which direction do the probabilities move?
predict.answer: Calibration is lost: probabilities no longer track accuracy and become over-confident, piling onto the preferred answer, because the model is now a reward-maximizing policy rather than a probabilistic model.
predict.why: Maximizing a reward concentrates mass on high-reward outputs (mode collapse, entropy drops) regardless of the model's epistemic uncertainty.
predict.targets_misconception: An RLHF model's token probability for an answer is its confidence that the answer is correct.

transfer.q: A team wants to use an RLHF chat model to estimate how likely a fact is true by reading off its next-token probability for 'yes'. Using p32 and p64, say why this is unreliable and propose one measurement that does not rely on the policy's probabilities being calibrated.
transfer.answer: The RLHF model is a policy optimized for preferred outputs, not a model of a distribution, so its probabilities are not calibrated. Instead: sample many answers and measure agreement, ask the model to output a verbal confidence and calibrate it on held-out data, or use the base (pre-RLHF) model's probabilities.
transfer.why: Calibration requires a probabilistic model of the data; RLHF deliberately abandons that in favour of reward maximization.
transfer.varies: functional: the probabilities are used for uncertainty estimation rather than generation
transfer.invariant: an RLHF model's probabilities encode reward preference, not frequency of correctness

check.why: p64: RLHF makes models no longer probabilistic models, with no calibration by default; p32: the RLHF model is a policy, not a model of a distribution. Mode collapse means entropy drops toward high-reward modes, not that outputs become nonsense.
check.varies: a quantitative accuracy readout from the probabilities instead of a proposal to read off P('yes')
